summary: Re-verify the 54 cost-explorer audit findings: each adversarially checked against the real code by an independent verifier
logs: Re-verifying 54 findings, one independent verifier each

confirmed.title: EC2 per-region CE query has no REGION filter, so the same account-wide EC2 cost is counted once per region
confirmed.reasoning: The mechanism holds against the real code. runner.py:84 creates one CE client ce_raw = session.client("ce", region_name="us-east-1") and passes it to attribute_ec2_account once (runner.py:108-110) with the full regions list and spec. attribute_ec2_account (ec2.py:53-56) loops over every region and calls _attribute_from_usage_type with that same ce_raw client and same spec each time. Inside _attribute_from_usage_type the CE filter (ec2.py:72-79) is built from base_filter = build_ce_filter(spec) AND {Dimensions: SERVICE = "Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud - Compute"}. I confirmed in core/filters.py that build_ce_filter never emits a REGION dimension, and the default spec pre_credit_gross() only excludes Credit/Refund/Upfront record types. The region parameter is used ONLY for ec2.client(region_name=region) instance enumeration (ec2.py:121) and the region= output field (ec2.py:174, 200) — never in the CE query. Therefore every per-region get_cost_and_usage call returns the identical account-wide cost-by-USAGE_TYPE; line 102 strips the region prefix from keys (e.g. USE1-BoxUsage:t3.micro -> BoxUsage:t3.micro), collapsing all regions' usage into one ce_by_key dict, the same on every iteration. Each region call then allocates that full account-wide ce_cost across only that region's instances (ec2.py:161-165). I verified runner.py has NO EC2 rescaling step: rescaling exists only for EBS/EIP against "EC2 - Other" (runner.py:164-175) and for RDS/ELB (runner.py:177-189). EC2 rows flow unmodified into flat (runner.py:216-220). One refinement to the finding's "Nx" claim: inflation only occurs for usage buckets that have matching instances in a given region — a (lifecycle, itype) bucket with no instances in region R contributes nothing there (ec2.py:184-208 only emit rows for stopped instances). So the exact over-count depends on instance-type/region overlap, but any account running the same instance types in multiple regions (common) gets that bucket's full account-wide cost counted once per overlapping region, materially inflating the headline EC2 total.
confirmed.evidence: aws_cost_ultra/resources/runner.py:84 (single us-east-1 ce_raw); runner.py:108-110 (one call with regions list); aws_cost_ultra/resources/ec2.py:53-56 (per-region loop, same ce_raw+spec); ec2.py:72-79 (filter = base spec + SERVICE only, no REGION); ec2.py:91-96 (GroupBy USAGE_TYPE, no REGION); ec2.py:102 (region prefix stripped, proving account-wide response); ec2.py:121,150-165 (full ce_cost split over one region's instances); core/filters.py:80-144 (build_ce_filter never adds REGION); core/filters.py:159-168 (default spec excludes only record types); runner.py:164-189 (rescaling only for EBS/EIP/RDS/ELB — none for EC2); runner.py:216-220 (EC2 rows enter flat unrescaled).
confirmed.fix_note: Correct: add a REGION dimension to the per-iteration CE filter (And SERVICE with {Dimensions:{Key:'REGION',Values:[region]}}), or query CE once with GroupBy [USAGE_TYPE, REGION] and partition by region before splitting across that region's instances.
confirmed.description: attribute_ec2_account loops over every region and calls _attribute_from_usage_type once per region. Inside, the CE GetCostAndUsage filter (lines 72-79) contains only the base spec filter plus a SERVICE=EC2-Compute dimension — there is NO REGION dimension. The CE client is the single us-east-1 raw client passed down from runner.py (ce_raw), so each per-region call returns the SAME global EC2 cost-by-usage-type. The code then enumerates instances only in that region and allocates the global CE cost across them. Across N regions this attributes roughly N times the true EC2 spend in aggregate (each region's instances get a slice of the full account total). The USAGE_TYPE keys do carry a region prefix that is stripped (line 102), confirming the response is account-wide, not region-scoped.
confirmed.scenario: An account running EC2 in 3 regions: real EC2 cost is $300. enumerate_all(region='all') calls _attribute_from_usage_type 3 times, each seeing the full $300 split by usage type, and each splitting that $300 across only that region's running instances. Summed EC2 attributed cost approaches $900 (3x), and since EC2 has no later CE-total rescaling step (only EBS/EIP, RDS/ELB are rescaled), the inflated total flows straight to the dashboard.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Add a REGION dimension to the CE filter keyed to the loop's region (And the SERVICE filter with {Dimensions:{Key:'REGION',Values:[region]}}), or query CE once with GroupBy [USAGE_TYPE, REGION] and partition results by region before splitting across that region's instances.

confirmed.title: Reflected XSS: profile/period query params raw-interpolated into inline <script> in trend-chart
confirmed.reasoning: The cited code is exactly as described. api_trend_chart (cost.py:362-370) takes profile and period as untyped FastAPI Query params (default str, no constraint/regex/enum), builds data_url via f-string at line 363, then embeds data_url unescaped inside an inline ). The route is independently reachable as GET /api/cost/trend-chart and also wired via hx-get from dashboard.html:66, so a crafted link is a real reflected-XSS delivery vector. Mechanism clearly holds. Impact caveat: serve() defaults host to 127.0.0.1 (app.py:97), so by default this is a localhost dashboard — exploitation requires luring the local operator to click an attacker-crafted localhost URL; with the dashboard running against live AWS credentials, executed script can drive same-origin /api/cost CE calls or exfiltrate page data (account IDs, ARNs, costs). The localhost binding tempers but does not eliminate the risk (reflected XSS via crafted link is exactly this model, and host is overridable), so high stands.
confirmed.evidence: aws_cost_ultra/web/routes/cost.py:362-370 (data_url f-string at 363, unescaped fetch("{data_url}") inside inline <script> at 366, HTMLResponse(html) at 370); aws_cost_ultra/web/deps.py:190 (mapping.get(period, current_month) — no rejection of unknown period); aws_cost_ultra/web/app.py:31 (only CECountingMiddleware, no CSP/security headers); aws_cost_ultra/web/templates/dashboard.html:66 (hx-get to /api/cost/trend-chart). Route also reachable directly via GET.
confirmed.fix_note: Proposed fix is correct: build the URL with urllib.parse.urlencode and emit it into a data-* attribute on the canvas read by static JS (charts.js already has the trend-canvas pattern at charts.js:169), never interpolating request input into a <script> body; additionally validate profile against profile_choices and period against an explicit allow-list.
confirmed.description: api_trend_chart builds an HTML fragment with an f-string: data_url = f"/api/cost/trend/data?profile={profile}&period={period}" and then embeds it directly inside an inline <script> as fetch("{data_url}"). Both `profile` and `period` are attacker-controlled Query params with NO validation, escaping, or allow-listing anywhere in the request path (period_to_window/deps.py just .get(period, current_month) and never rejects unknown values). Because the value lands inside a JS string literal in an inline <script>, an attacker can break out of the string and the script context. Returned via HTMLResponse with no escaping. The route is reachable directly by URL (GET /api/cost/trend-chart) and via hx-get from pages, so a crafted link is a classic reflected-XSS delivery vector against any dashboard operator who clicks it; the dashboard runs against live AWS credentials, so script execution can pivot to triggering money-spending CE/describe calls or exfiltrating page contents (account IDs, ARNs, cost data).
confirmed.scenario: Operator opens /api/cost/trend-chart?profile=%22)%3B%7Dalert(document.domain)%3B(()%3D%3E%7Bfetch(%22&period=3m (i.e. profile = "");}alert(document.domain);(()=>{fetch("). The injected text closes the fetch() string and statement, runs alert/arbitrary JS, then re-opens a call so the rest of the template still parses. Same applies to period. Even simpler: profile=" closes the inline script tag and injects an HTML element with an event handler.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Do not interpolate user input into inline script/HTML. Either (a) JSON-encode and additionally escape script-breaking sequences, e.g. build the URL with urllib.parse.urlencode({"profile": profile, "period": period}) and inject via a data-* attribute on the canvas that charts.js reads, or (b) validate profile against the known profile_choices list and period against an explicit allow-list (mtd/last_month/30d/3m/...) and 400 on anything else, plus HTML-escape before embedding. Best: emit the URL into a data attribute and have static JS read it, never building <script> bodies from request input.

confirmed.title: S3 attribution makes per-bucket get_bucket_location + get_bucket_tagging + CloudWatch calls for ALL buckets in EVERY region
confirmed.reasoning: The mechanism holds exactly as described. In runner.py:135 the S3 attribution is dispatched through `_fanout_regions(attribute_s3, ce_total("S3"))`, which (runner.py:112-124) submits one call to `attribute_s3` per region in `regions` (from `accessible_regions`, session.py:142-152, which returns all opted-in regions — up to ~20+). Each invocation of `attribute_s3` (s3.py:27-29) calls the GLOBAL `list_buckets()`, returning every bucket in the account every time. Then s3.py:37-45 loops over ALL buckets calling `get_bucket_location` to filter to the current region — that is O(B) location calls per region invocation, i.e. O(B*R) globally. With B=5000 buckets and R=20 regions this is 100,000 get_bucket_location calls, matching the trigger scenario. For surviving in-region buckets, s3.py:56-77 issues a sequential `get_metric_statistics` per bucket (no bounded concurrency) and s3.py:95-99 issues `get_bucket_tagging` per bucket. Error handling silently drops/degrades: `get_bucket_location` ClientError -> `continue` (s3.py:44-45) drops the bucket entirely from attribution, and `get_bucket_tagging` ClientError -> `pass` (s3.py:98-99) leaves it untagged. Under throttling (very likely at this call volume, all running under the concurrent region fan-out via _frozen_session threads), these swallowed errors cause inconsistent bucket drops and missing tags/names. No guard prevents this: there is no per-region bucket grouping, no location cache, and no short-circuit — `attribute_s3` is region-agnostic in its inputs and re-does the full global scan every time. I could not find any invariant that refutes the bug.
confirmed.evidence: runner.py:135 (`jobs["s3"] = pool.submit(_fanout_regions, attribute_s3, ...)`), runner.py:112-118 (per-region submit loop), session.py:142-152 (accessible_regions returns all opted-in regions). s3.py:29 (global `list_buckets()`), s3.py:37-45 (per-bucket `get_bucket_location` over ALL buckets, ClientError->continue drops bucket), s3.py:56-77 (sequential per-bucket `get_metric_statistics`), s3.py:95-99 (`get_bucket_tagging`, ClientError->pass leaves untagged).
confirmed.fix_note: Fix is correct in substance: list_buckets once globally, resolve+cache each bucket's region once, group by region before dispatch. Minor inaccuracy: Lambda is NOT bounded (lambda_fn.py:56 is a plain sequential loop) so "as already done for Lambda/DynamoDB" overstates existing bounding; still, bounding the CloudWatch fan-out / GetMetricData batching is a valid additional improvement.
confirmed.description: list_buckets is global, so attribute_s3 is invoked once per region by the fan-out, and each invocation calls get_bucket_location for EVERY bucket in the account (line 39) to filter to the current region, then for the surviving buckets calls get_metric_statistics (line 59) and get_bucket_tagging (line 96). With B buckets and R regions this is O(B*R) get_bucket_location calls plus O(B) CloudWatch + tagging calls per region. For an account with thousands of buckets across 20 regions this is tens of thousands of S3/CloudWatch API calls, heavily throttle-prone and slow, all under the concurrent region fan-out. get_bucket_location/get_bucket_tagging throttling is silently swallowed (continue/pass), so buckets get dropped or untagged inconsistently.
confirmed.scenario: Account with 5,000 S3 buckets and 20 opted-in regions. The S3 fan-out runs attribute_s3 20 times; each calls get_bucket_location 5,000 times = 100,000 location calls, plus CloudWatch per in-region bucket. This dominates runtime and trips S3 request throttling, causing buckets to be silently dropped from attribution.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Call list_buckets once globally, resolve each bucket's region once (cache location), and group buckets by region before dispatching, rather than re-listing and re-locating all buckets in every region worker. Bound the CloudWatch fan-out (as already done for Lambda/DynamoDB) and consider GetMetricData batching.

confirmed.title: Month-end forecast drops the remainder of today (forecast window starts tomorrow midnight)
confirmed.reasoning: The mechanism holds exactly as described, and the date-granularity of CE queries makes it slightly worse. In cost.py:52-99, fcast_window = remainder_of_current_month() and ctx['forecast'] = mtd_amount + forecast_cv.amount_usd, where mtd_amount comes from current_month() (time_windows.py:26-30, start=1st-midnight, end=now). remainder_of_current_month() (time_windows.py:56-62) sets start=(now+1day).replace(hour=0,...) = tomorrow midnight UTC. So the two windows are MTD=[month-1st 00:00, now] and forecast=[tomorrow 00:00, next-month-1st]. The interval [now, tomorrow 00:00] is in neither, producing a systematic under-projection. Critically, both windows are passed to CE via window.iso() (types.py:56-58), which formats Start/End as YYYY-MM-DD (date only). CE cost queries are half-open on dates, so the MTD actual matrix only covers full days up through yesterday (End=today's date excludes today), and the forecast Start=tomorrow's date. The net effect is the ENTIRE current calendar day's spend is omitted from the projected month total (not just the partial remainder), except in the degenerate case where now is exactly midnight. Only one caller exists and no compensating partial-day actual is added back.
confirmed.evidence: aws_cost_ultra/core/time_windows.py:56-62 (start = (now + timedelta(days=1)).replace(hour=0,...)); time_windows.py:26-30 (current_month end=now); aws_cost_ultra/web/routes/cost.py:52-53,62,99 (fcast_window=remainder_of_current_month(); mtd_window=current_month(); ctx['forecast']=mtd_amount+forecast_cv.amount_usd); aws_cost_ultra/aws/cost_explorer.py:273,284 (start_s,end_s = window.iso(); TimePeriod Start/End); aws_cost_ultra/core/types.py:56-58 (iso() returns YYYY-MM-DD date strings).
confirmed.fix_note: Fix is directionally correct but must respect CE's date granularity: forecast Start should be today's date (the same date MTD's End covers, since MTD excludes today), i.e. start = _utc_today_midnight(), not tomorrow. CE's get_cost_forecast allows Start = today, so the partial day is forecast rather than dropped; alternatively add a same-day actual query. Note the gap is a whole calendar day, not just the partial remainder, so the under-projection can be a full day's spend.
confirmed.description: remainder_of_current_month() starts the forecast window at tomorrow 00:00 UTC (start = (now + 1 day).replace(hour=0...)). In cost.py _build_summary_ctx the month-end projection is computed as ctx['forecast'] = mtd_amount + forecast_cv.amount_usd, where mtd_amount = current_month().total() covers [1st 00:00, now]. The interval [now, tomorrow 00:00 UTC] (the rest of today) is covered by NEITHER the MTD actual NOR the forecast window. The projected month total therefore systematically omits the cost of the current partial day, under-projecting end-of-month spend.
confirmed.scenario: Account spending ~$10k/day. User loads the summary at 02:00 UTC. MTD actual covers up to 02:00; forecast covers tomorrow-midnight onward. ~22 hours of today's spend (~$9k) is in the projected-month figure's blind spot, so the forecast card reads ~$9k low versus what the AWS console projects. The gap is largest early in the UTC day.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Start the forecast window at the current MTD window's end (now, the same instant MTD stops) rather than at tomorrow midnight, e.g. start = now (or the next CE-allowed boundary) so [MTD end, forecast start] has no gap; or add the partial-day actual explicitly. Ensure CE's Start>=today constraint is still satisfied.

confirmed.title: Previous-period comparison uses a calendar month against a non-month window (length mismatch)
confirmed.reasoning: The code matches the finding exactly. In cost.py:50-51, window = period_to_window(period) and prev_window = period_to_window("last_month") if period in ("mtd","3m","30d") else period_to_window("3m"). In deps.py:178-189 the mapping confirms: "3m" -> last_n_days(90), "30d" -> last_n_days(30), "mtd" -> current_month(), "last_month" -> last_month(). In time_windows.py: last_n_days(n) spans n days ending at now (line 20-23); last_month() is a full calendar month [1st, 1st-of-next) i.e. ~28-31 days (line 33-39); current_month() is 1st-of-month to now (1-31 days). cost_store.py:45-46 total() is a raw sum over all daily cells with NO per-day normalization, so a longer window mechanically sums more spend. change_pct = (total_amount - prev_amount)/prev_amount*100 (cost.py:96) therefore compares window sums of different lengths/alignment. For period="3m": current = 90-day sum vs prev = ~30-day calendar-month sum, roughly a 3x inflation that surfaces as a fake ~+200% spike. For "30d": 30-rolling-day vs full-calendar-month (28-31 days) — smaller but still a length+alignment mismatch. The clamp at line 97 (max(-999.9, min(9999.9, raw))) and the prev>=0.50 guard at line 95 do NOT correct the mismatch; they only bound an already-wrong number. The value is consumed directly: App.jsx:157 renders delta={value(s.change_pct)} on the "Period spend" KPI labeled note="vs previous period", and cost_cards.html:28-31 renders an up/down arrow with fmt_pct. The same defect exists in _build_services_ctx (cost.py:117) feeding per-service row.change_pct (service_table.html, App.jsx:347). Periods are user-selectable (App.jsx:90-91 dropdown; "3m" labeled "rolling 3 months" at App.jsx:36), so the trigger is reachable in normal use. The only nuance vs the finding: even "mtd" vs "last_month" is partial-month-vs-full-month and also mismatched, so the bug is broader than just 3m/30d, but the 3m case (90 vs 30 days) is the most severe and is real.
confirmed.evidence: aws_cost_ultra/web/routes/cost.py:50-51 (window/prev_window selection), cost.py:96 (change_pct formula), cost.py:117 (same in services); aws_cost_ultra/web/deps.py:185 ("3m" -> last_n_days(90)), deps.py:180,183 (30d/last_month); aws_cost_ultra/core/time_windows.py:20-23 (last_n_days), 33-39 (last_month full calendar month); aws_cost_ultra/aws/cost_store.py:45-46 (total() raw unnormalized sum); frontend/src/App.jsx:157 (change_pct shown "vs previous period"), App.jsx:36 ("3m" = "rolling 3 months")
confirmed.fix_note: Proposed fix is correct: derive prev_window with the same length/alignment as the current window (preceding N-day window for rolling periods; prior calendar month vs full last_month only when current is a full month). Have period_to_window return the window length so the comparison window can mirror it.
confirmed.description: prev_window = period_to_window('last_month') if period in ('mtd','3m','30d') else period_to_window('3m'). For period='30d' the current window is last_n_days(30) (a rolling 30-day window via deps.period_to_window), but the previous window is last_month() — a full calendar month (28-31 days, fixed [1st,1st)). change_pct = (total - prev)/prev*100 then compares a trailing-30-day sum against a calendar-month sum of different length and different alignment. For period='3m' it is worse: the current window is last_n_days(90) (90 days) compared against last_month() (~30 days), so change_pct compares ~90 days of spend to ~30 days — roughly a 3x inflation that looks like a +200% spike.
confirmed.scenario: User selects the '3m' period. Current window = 90 days (~$30k), prev = last calendar month (~$10k). change_pct = (30000-10000)/10000*100 = +200%, displayed as a massive cost increase that is purely an artifact of comparing windows of different length.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Derive the previous window from the SAME window length/granularity as the current one (e.g., for an N-day rolling window, prev = the immediately preceding N-day window; for mtd, prev = same-day-of-month range of prior month or full last month with an explicit 'partial vs full' note). Make period_to_window return the length so the comparison window can mirror it.

confirmed.title: Services-page prev-period map mismatched for 3m and uses calendar month for 30d
confirmed.reasoning: Read the real code. cost.py:117 sets prev_window = period_to_window("last_month") if period in ("mtd","30d") else period_to_window("3m"). deps.py:178-191 maps both "3m" and the else-branch to last_n_days(90), and the current window for period="3m" is also period_to_window("3m")=last_n_days(90) (cost.py:116). time_windows.last_n_days (lines 20-23) is a pure function of now/today, so the two calls produce the same rolling 90-day window covering the same UTC days. cost_store.by_service() (lines 48-52) aggregates per-service cell totals over that window, so prev_map equals the current per-service totals. In service_rows_from_groups (service_groups.py:60-64), change_pct = (cost-prev)/prev*100 = 0 for every service when prev==cost. So for period="3m" every service shows ~0% change regardless of real MoM movement. (a) For "30d": current = rolling last_n_days(30) but prev = last_month() calendar month (28-31 days) — length/alignment mismatch, deltas distorted. (b) For "6m"/"12m": current = trailing_months(6/12) (months-long) but prev = last_n_days(90) (only 90 days) — nonsensical ratio. The one case the finding overstates is "mtd": prev=last_month is a legitimate calendar MoM comparison, so that branch is fine. Note this also diverges from _build_summary_ctx line 51 which includes "3m" in the last_month branch, so the summary card and the services table use different prev windows for 3m — an internal inconsistency. Mechanism clearly holds; no guard or validation prevents it (period is a free-form Query string with no whitelist).

Note 'mtd' and '30d' both map prev to last_month() (calendar month), while every other period (including '3m'=90 days, '6m', '12m') maps prev to period_to_window('3m')=last_n_days(90). confirmed.title: Trend table/data endpoints ignore the configured cost basis (no pre_credit_gross spec)
confirmed.reasoning: The mechanism holds exactly as described. In aws_cost_ultra/web/routes/cost.py, api_trend_data (line 349) calls ce.get_trend(window, granularity=gran, spec=spec) with spec=pre_credit_gross() (line 347), which sets excluded_record_types=("Credit","Refund","Upfront"). By contrast api_trend_table (line 390) and api_trend_table_data (line 417) both call ce.get_trend(window, granularity=gran) with NO spec argument. get_trend (cost_explorer.py:217-220) declares spec: Optional[CostFilterSpec]=None and then executes `spec = spec or console_default()`. console_default() (filters.py:151-156) returns an empty CostFilterSpec(), which CE treats as "include everything (net after credits)". So the table endpoints genuinely use a different cost basis (net after credits) than the chart endpoint (pre-credit gross). This is not theoretical: the Trends page template (trends.html lines 18-19 and 30-31) renders BOTH the chart (/api/cost/trend/data) and the table (/api/cost/trend-table) for the identical {{ period }} and {{ active_profile }} on the same page. On a credit-heavy or RI-upfront account the chart bars (gross) and the table cost column (net) will diverge by the credit/refund/upfront amount for the same months. The summary cards (line 44) and services tables (lines 114, 274) all use pre_credit_gross() and emit cost_basis_label (lines 39, 148, 316), but the trend-table contexts (ctx at lines 385, 412) have neither the matching spec nor any cost_basis_label, so the user gets no indication the basis changed. No guard, validation, or invariant prevents this. The only mitigating factor is that the divergence is zero on accounts with no credits/refunds/upfront RI, but for the stated trigger (credit/RI-heavy accounts) the numbers visibly mismatch — exactly the trust break the pre-credit basis design exists to prevent.
confirmed.evidence: cost.py:347-349 (api_trend_data uses spec=pre_credit_gross()); cost.py:390 and cost.py:417 (get_trend called with no spec); cost_explorer.py:217,220 (spec=None default then `spec = spec or console_default()`); filters.py:151-156 (console_default returns empty CostFilterSpec = all record types) vs filters.py:159-168 (pre_credit_gross excludes Credit/Refund/Upfront); trends.html:18-19 and 30-31 (chart and table rendered same page, same period/profile); cost.py:39,148,316 (cost_basis_label set elsewhere) vs cost.py:385,412 (trend-table ctx has no cost_basis_label).
confirmed.fix_note: Correct: add spec=pre_credit_gross() to get_trend at cost.py:390 and 417, and set ctx["cost_basis_label"] in both trend-table contexts to match the chart/summary basis.
confirmed.description: api_trend_table (line 390) and api_trend_table_data (line 417) call ce.get_trend(window, granularity=gran) with NO spec, so get_trend falls back to console_default() = all record types (net after credits). Meanwhile api_trend_data (line 349), the summary cards, and the services tables all use spec=pre_credit_gross() (excludes Credit/Refund/Upfront). The same trend, rendered as a chart vs a table, therefore uses two different cost bases. On a credit-heavy or RI-upfront account the table totals will differ from the chart and from the summary card for the same period, exactly the 'numbers don't match' trust break the provenance design is meant to prevent. confirmed.title: CE-total rescaling factor can divide by a near-zero raw_sum, massively inflating per-resource cost
confirmed.reasoning:
The rescaling code is exactly as cited (runner.py:164-189): EBS/EIP use factor = other_pool/raw_sum, RDS/ELB use factor = ce_tot/raw_sum, guarded ONLY by `raw_sum > 0` with no clamp on factor magnitude, then multiplied onto every row. The output flows to the user-facing resources API (resources_api.py:72) and ce_total_by_service holds real Cost Explorer service totals (runner.py:89). So an unbounded factor multiplying nonzero rows while leaving zero-cost rows at 0 is a real, reachable misattribution.

The finding's SPECIFIC root cause is partly wrong, though. Unknown-type pricing does NOT fall back to $0 for the pools in question: ebs_rate defaults unknown volume types to gp3 (pricing.py:162), elb_rate defaults to application (line 192), rds_storage_rate defaults to gp2 (line 182) — all nonzero. The cited 'EBS type missing from FALLBACK_RATES prices at $0' scenario cannot occur. Only ec2_on_demand_rate (line 144, EC2 not in these pools) and rds_instance_rate (line 172) actually return 0.0 for unknown keys.

However the tiny-raw_sum mechanism is still reachable via a different, realistic path: hours_between returns 0.0 when the effective window collapses (base.py:75), and RDS forces hrs=0 for any instance not in 'available' state (rds.py:41) which zeroes instance cost; combined with rds_instance_rate=0.0 for an unknown class and 0 storage, an RDS row can be exactly $0. Accounts commonly have many stopped DB instances. If most rows in a service/region pool are zero-cost (stopped DBs, EBS volumes created after window end) and one is small-but-nonzero, raw_sum is tiny and factor explodes, dumping the entire CE service pool onto the one nonzero row. EIP is exempt because every EIP gets identical cost = window_hours*0.005 (eip.py:37), so the EIP side can't be the lone-nonzero row, but the EBS side of EC2-Other and the RDS/ELB pools all qualify.

Net: the bug CLASS (unbounded rescale factor + zero-cost rows -> gross misattribution, plus silent rescaling instead of surfacing drift) is confirmed and user-visible, but the trigger is narrower than described (requires a skewed mix of zero-cost and one tiny nonzero row in the same pool) and the everyday effect of this code is moderate over/under-scaling rather than the extreme 200000x case, so medium not high.

confirmed.title: CE call counter does not propagate into ThreadPoolExecutor worker threads; X-CE-Calls-Spent severely undercounts
confirmed.reasoning: The mechanism holds exactly as described. The CE counter is incremented only inside cost_explorer CE calls via get_current_counter().add(...) at cost_explorer.py:295 (get_forecast) and cost_explorer.py:392-395 (_get_cost_and_usage, the pagination loop that backs daily_service_matrix/get_matrix/get_total_cost). The counter lives in a module-level ContextVar with default=None (middleware.py:32). CECountingMiddleware.dispatch sets it on the async request task and reads back its own `counter` object into the headers (middleware.py:46-53). FastAPI/anyio copies the request context into the endpoint's sync threadpool worker, so a CE call made directly in the endpoint body — e.g. ce.get_total_cost at resources_api.py:92 — IS counted correctly. BUT the summary/services endpoints dispatch get_matrix and ce.get_forecast into a nested plain ThreadPoolExecutor (cost.py:59-66 max_workers=4, cost.py:121-123 max_workers=2) and the SWR background refresh uses _refresh_pool (deps.py:70,99). I empirically verified that a plain ThreadPoolExecutor.submit() does NOT propagate contextvars: the worker sees the default (None) while main still sees the request value. So inside those pool workers, get_current_counter() finds None and lazily creates a throwaway CECallCounter (middleware.py:37-41) bound to the worker thread's own (default) context; it is never merged back into the request counter the middleware reads. There is no contextvars.copy_context() wrapping anywhere in the codebase (grep confirms zero hits). Net: every CE page issued for matrices and the forecast on these endpoints is invisible to X-CE-Calls-Spent / X-CE-Estimated-Cost-USD. Impact is real but bounded by caching: get_matrix only calls CE on a cold/forced cache (cost_store.py:118-122); on a warm cache no CE call occurs and 0 is genuinely correct. So the under-count manifests on cold cache (the moments CE is actually billed) and for the forecast (always uncounted when it runs in the pool). The headers are a developer/operator visibility aid, not a correctness-critical or security boundary, hence medium rather than high.

A plain ThreadPoolExecutor does NOT copy contextvars into its worker threads (verified: a worker sees the ContextVar default, not the request value). Inside those workers, cost_explorer._get_cost_and_usage calls get_current_counter() which sees None and lazily creates a brand-new throwaway CECallCounter in the worker's own context (middleware.py:38-41). The response counter the middleware reads only reflects CE calls made directly on the request thread (e.g. ce.get_forecast at cost.py:62 also runs in the pool, so it's lost too; ce.get_total_cost in resources_api runs on the request thread so it counts). Open windows produced by time_windows.current_month()/last_n_days() set `end = datetime.now(tz=utc)` (time_windows.py:23,30), so their iso end-date == the current UTC date. These open windows are exactly what the routes request: deps.py:179-185 maps mtd→current_month and 30d/60d/90d/3m→last_n_days, and the default is current_month (deps.py:190); all flow through cost.py:60/64/122 → src.get_matrix → CostStore.get_matrix → _is_closed_window (cost_store.py:129).

Because the test uses `<=` and a date-only comparison, an open window whose end date equals today's date is classified CLOSED. On a UTC-clock server, date.today()==current UTC date, so an open mtd/30d window satisfies `end <= today` → CLOSED → ttl=30d, swr=0 (cost_store.py:130). The cache then serves the stale partial total via cache_get→SqliteCache.get (sqlite_cache.py:67-78, returns value while age<ttl). So a partial current-period total fetched early in the UTC day is frozen and reused for the rest of that UTC day with no 15-min refresh — the data-accuracy harm the finding describes. (The key embeds the UTC end-date, so it self-corrects at UTC midnight; the freeze is bounded to the current UTC day, not literally 30 days.)

The finding's specific tz claim is actually inverted: for a server BEHIND UTC near local midnight, the UTC end-date is a day AHEAD of local date, so `end <= today(local)` is False → correctly OPEN — that case mitigates rather than triggers the freeze. For servers AHEAD of UTC, end-date(UTC) can be a day behind local date, making the mis-classification even more aggressive. But the bug fires regardless of timezone (even pure UTC) due to the `<=`, so it is confirmed, not refuted.

confirmed.title: SWR refresh pool (max_workers=4) saturates across many keys; deduped-but-still-serialized refreshes starve and never-refresh hot keys
confirmed.reasoning:
The core mechanism is real. deps.py:70 creates a single module-global _refresh_pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) shared across every SWR key. schedule_refresh (deps.py:75-99) dedupes per-key via _refreshing/_refresh_lock, then calls _refresh_pool.submit(_run) (deps.py:99) with no in-flight cap, no shedding, and no producer timeout. Python's stdlib ThreadPoolExecutor uses an unbounded SimpleQueue, so submit never blocks or rejects — excess tasks queue without bound. The producers are genuinely heavy: build_resources_ctx (resources_api.py:44-100) calls enumerate_all (runner.py:64-150), which resolves all opted-in regions and fans describe calls across them plus CE queries; build_audit_ctx is similarly heavy. With many distinct keys going stale at once, at most 4 run concurrently and the rest queue. With no per-producer timeout, a single hung/throttled describe permanently ties up one of the 4 worker threads, shrinking effective capacity. The id(session) growth is also real: get_session (deps.py:106-112) builds a fresh boto3 Session each refresh, so id(session) (deps.py:127) differs every time and the per-thread _ce_local.clients dict (deps.py:128-135) accumulates one CostExplorerClient per refresh on the long-lived pool threads, never cleared — a slow leak.

Two parts of the finding are overstated, which is why I keep it at medium rather than high: (1) The SWR cache key is resources:{profile}:{period}:{region} (resources_api.py:112) and region is normally ALL_REGIONS ("all") — so the 30 regions multiply work INSIDE a single refresh task, not into 30 distinct keys. Distinct keys are roughly profiles x periods (plus audit keys), i.e. dozens, not the "hundreds" claimed. (2) Serving stale during a backlog is by-design SWR behavior, not a correctness bug — users see slightly old numbers, not wrong ones, and a starved key is re-cached once its queued task eventually runs (not literally "never" unless re-scheduled faster than the queue drains). So the realistic harm is degraded freshness and a worker-exhaustion risk under large multi-profile load plus slow per-thread memory growth — a genuine scalability/resource-management weakness, but not a data-correctness or security issue.

confirmed.title: CE call counter undercounts: contextvar not propagated to ThreadPoolExecutor workers
confirmed.reasoning: The mechanism is real and I reproduced its root cause empirically. (1) The request counter is a contextvars.ContextVar set only in CECountingMiddleware.dispatch (middleware.py:46-47), and the response headers are written from that same request-scoped `counter` local (middleware.py:52-53). (2) get_current_counter (middleware.py:35-41) returns _current.get(), and if it is None it fabricates a NEW throwaway counter and sets it in the *current* context only. (3) In _build_summary_ctx (cost.py:59-66) ALL four CE-capable calls — 3x src.get_matrix and 1x ce.get_forecast — are dispatched via pool.submit on a plain concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor; there are zero direct CE calls on the handler thread for this endpoint. _build_services_ctx (cost.py:121-123) does the same for its 2 matrix fetches. (4) On a cold cache miss, CostStore.get_matrix (cost_store.py:117-125) actually invokes self._ce.daily_service_matrix -> _get_cost_and_usage (cost_explorer.py:392-395) and get_forecast (cost_explorer.py:294-295) call get_current_counter().add(...) from inside those worker threads. (5) I empirically verified that ThreadPoolExecutor.submit does NOT copy the submitting thread's context: a worker reads the ContextVar default (None) even after the submitter calls set(). So inside each pool worker get_current_counter() finds None, manufactures an orphan counter, and all pages/records are written there, never to the request counter. The header therefore reports 0 calls / $0.00000 on a cold summary/services request even though several deeply-paginated CE calls really happened. The contrast endpoints (/services/composition/data cost.py:276, /trend/data cost.py:349) call CE directly on the handler thread — where anyio already copied the middleware's context — so those count correctly, which is exactly consistent with the finding that only the pool-using endpoints undercount. Refute attempt failed: there is no guard, no explicit counter passing, and no context-copy wrapper anywhere. Impact: this is an observability/cost-estimate inaccuracy, not a correctness or security issue — the displayed cost numbers and dashboard data are unaffected; only the diagnostic X-CE-Calls-Spent / X-CE-Estimated-Cost-USD headers are wrong, and wrong worst on large cold accounts. That undermines the counter's stated purpose but causes no functional or financial harm, so high is too strong; medium is calibrated.

confirmed.title: Per-thread CostExplorerClient cache keyed by id(session) leaks unboundedly and risks id reuse
confirmed.reasoning: The leak mechanism is real. get_ce_client caches a CostExplorerClient in a per-thread dict keyed by id(session) and never evicts (deps.py:127-135). get_session (deps.py:106-112) calls make_session, which constructs a brand-new boto3.Session() on every call (session.py:75-83), so every request yields a session with a distinct id(). confirmed.title: SqliteCache opens a new connection per operation and never closes it
confirmed.reasoning: The core mechanism is real and verified both by reading code and empirically. SqliteCache._connect() (sqlite_cache.py:49-55) does sqlite3.connect() plus two PRAGMA statements on every call, and every cache op (get:68, get_swr:81/95, set:60, bust:103, _init_db:41/46) uses `with self._connect() as conn:`. The sqlite3 Connection context manager only commits/rolls back; it does NOT close the connection — confirmed correct. The cache is a module-level singleton (deps.py:32 `_cache = SqliteCache(...)`), reached on the hot path of every cost route (cost.py:161-424, resources_api, audit_api, context.py, cost_store.get_matrix:118/134) and from the 4-worker acu-refresh ThreadPoolExecutor (deps.py:70,92). I initially hypothesized CPython refcounting would close each connection deterministically at method return, which would refute the finding. Empirical testing disproved my refutation: the `with conn as c:` pattern creates reference cycles (cursors/statements ref the connection), so connections are NOT freed by refcounting — with gc.disabled, ~2 FDs leak per op and 983 live Connection objects accumulated over 2000 ops; a single gc.collect() dropped them to 0 and FDs from 2008 to 4. So the finding's claim that connections release only on garbage collection (not deterministically) is correct. HOWEVER, the catastrophic impact is overstated: CPython's cyclic GC is enabled by default and triggers on allocation thresholds (gen0 ~700 net allocs), so connections stay bounded (a few hundred to low thousands transiently) rather than growing unboundedly — with GC on, 5000 ops plateaued at ~613 live conns / 1638 FDs. The system's soft FD ulimit here is 524288, far above any transient accumulation. The 'unable to open database file' / ulimit-exhaustion crash is unlikely under default CPython on this box, though it could bite on a low ulimit (e.g. 1024) under heavy bursts before a collection. The redundant per-op PRAGMA journal_mode/synchronous and connect cost is real wasted work but minor. Net: a genuine resource-management/efficiency defect, but not the high-severity unbounded-leak crash described.

refuted_or_false_positive.title: EC2 USAGE_TYPE parser drops us-east-1 (un-prefixed) usage types entirely
refuted_or_false_positive.reasoning:
The finding's headline claim — that un-prefixed (us-east-1) EC2 usage types are "dropped entirely" — is false, and the finding itself concedes this mid-description. The code at aws_cost_ultra/resources/ec2.py:102 is `rest = raw.split("-", 1)[1] if "-" in raw else raw`. For us-east-1, CE returns bare keys like `BoxUsage:t3.micro`, `SpotUsage:m5.large`, `HeavyUsage:c5.xlarge`. These contain no hyphen, so the guard `if "-" in raw` is False and `rest = raw` unchanged, which then correctly matches `startswith("BoxUsage:")` etc. at lines 103-108. So the un-prefixed path works exactly as intended.

The finding's secondary mechanism — a us-east-1 usage type "whose first token contains a hyphen" causing a mis-split — does not correspond to any real CE usage type. AWS EC2 instance-type identifiers (t3.micro, c5d.large, m5.large) use a dot, never a hyphen, in the family/size portion, and bare us-east-1 usage types have no leading region token at all. Thus `"-" in raw` is simply False for them and no split occurs.

For prefixed regions the prefix is a single token (APS3, EUW1, USE2, APN1) followed by exactly one hyphen, so `split("-", 1)[1]` cleanly strips it: `APS3-BoxUsage:t3.micro` -> `BoxUsage:t3.micro`. Works.

The `else: continue` at line 110 is intentional: this function only attributes compute-hour buckets (BoxUsage/SpotUsage/HeavyUsage). Non-hour usage types (EBS:VolumeUsage, DataTransfer, etc.) are deliberately skipped here because EBS/transfer are attributed elsewhere; they are not silently "dropped EC2 spend" being under-reported in a buggy way. There is no realistic CE key that both denotes per-instance-hour compute cost and fails this parser.
